ANO-2000.explanation_text: The reading jumped for a single hour in the middle of the night and then returned exactly to its normal level, with no build-up before and no elevated usage after. A genuine fault would have kept the unit running hard for several hours, and the mild overnight weather gives no reason for extra cooling demand. This pattern is characteristic of a bad individual meter reading rather than a real change in equipment behaviour, so no dispatch is needed, though a quick check of the meter's recent readings is worthwhile.

ANO-2001.explanation_text: Consumption on this HVAC unit jumped almost four times its normal level within a single hour and then stayed flat at that raised level for four hours, never easing back down. Outdoor conditions were steady and even eased slightly during the period, so the weather cannot account for the step change. A sudden jump that locks in at a high plateau is the signature of a failed or struggling fan forcing the unit to run continuously, and it should be inspected on site before the strain causes further damage.

ANO-2002.explanation_text: The reading jumped to roughly six times normal for a single hour on a cool evening, then fell straight back to normal levels with no gradual build-up or lingering elevated load. A genuine heating or cooling problem would keep drawing extra power after it started, and mild outdoor conditions on a Sunday evening give no reason for a real surge of that size. This pattern is characteristic of a bad reading from the meter rather than an actual change in equipment behaviour, so no dispatch is warranted, though a quick check that later readings stay normal is worthwhile.

ANO-2003.explanation_text: The unit's power draw jumped abruptly in the evening and stayed high for four hours with no sign of settling back down, even as outdoor conditions barely changed and the building was winding down for the night. That sustained step change points to the unit running continuously and struggling rather than responding to any real heating demand, which is typical of a failed or seized fan forcing the system to work against itself. A technician visit is warranted before the unit runs in this state overnight.

ANO-2004.explanation_text: The south lighting circuit jumped to more than triple its usual overnight level for a single hour late at night, then settled back on its own. That pattern points to the lighting controls briefly switching more of the array on than intended rather than to any night-time work activity, and the reading is well within what the circuit can physically draw so it is not a metering glitch. Worth adding to the controls check list and watching for repeats, but it does not need an immediate call-out.

ANO-2005.explanation_text: Power draw on this refrigeration zone climbed steadily over three hours in the early morning, well before any activity would explain it, and outdoor conditions were mild so weather is not the driver. A slow, progressive rise in cooling effort like this is the signature of a system losing cooling capacity and working ever harder to hold temperature, most commonly from a refrigerant loss. It is worth sending a technician promptly, as continued loss risks product temperature excursions and compressor damage.

ANO-2006.explanation_text: The lighting load jumped sharply for a single hour in the evening and then dropped straight back to normal, which looks like every lighting bank being energised at once rather than a gradual business-driven increase. The rise is large but still within what the lighting circuits could physically draw, and the evening hours afterwards show an unrelated step up in normal use, so this is not a metering error. The most likely cause is a lighting control or scheduling glitch that briefly overrode the normal timing, so it is worth checking the control panel logs and watching for a repeat rather than sending a crew immediately.

ANO-2007.explanation_text: The lighting circuit showed a single isolated hour of consumption far above what that set of fixtures can physically draw, then returned to normal immediately with no lingering elevation. An earlier erratic reading the same afternoon suggests the meter on this circuit is producing occasional false values. This looks like a measurement glitch rather than a real load, so no technician visit is needed, though the meter itself is worth checking if the pattern repeats.

ANO-2008.explanation_text: Power draw on this refrigeration zone stepped up sharply in the early morning and then kept climbing steadily over the following hours instead of settling back down. Outdoor conditions were cold, so weather and the start of the working day do not explain it — the unit is working progressively harder to hold temperature, which is the signature of a gradual loss of cooling capacity such as a refrigerant leak. This will keep worsening and risks product temperature excursions, so a technician should inspect the zone.

ANO-2009.explanation_text: Lighting load on the north grid jumped in the evening and then kept climbing rather than settling, staying elevated well past the point where the area should have been dark. The steady, escalating pattern with no return to normal points to lighting controls failing to switch circuits off or progressively bringing more zones on. It is worth having someone check the lighting control panel and schedule settings, though this can be handled during normal hours rather than as an emergency call-out.

ANO-2010.explanation_text: The unit's power draw jumped sharply overnight and then stayed high for several hours instead of settling back down. Outdoor conditions were mild and cooling, so there is no weather or business reason for the unit to work harder — the load should have been falling, not doubling. This pattern points to a mechanical problem in the air-handling side of the unit forcing it to run continuously, and a technician should check it.

ANO-2011.explanation_text: The unit jumped abruptly to roughly two and a half times its normal draw and then held steady there for a full eight hours without easing off. Outdoor conditions were cool and falling, so there is no weather or occupancy reason for the unit to be working this hard. A sudden step up that never recovers points to a mechanical failure inside the air handling side forcing the unit to run continuously, and it should be inspected promptly before it damages other components or drives further energy waste.

ANO-2012.explanation_text: The unit jumped abruptly to well above its normal overnight level and then stayed there for hours without drifting back down, while outdoor conditions stayed essentially flat. A step change that holds steady like this points to a mechanical problem in the air-handling side forcing the unit to work continuously rather than to weather or building activity. Recommend dispatching a technician to inspect the fan and airflow path before the unit runs another full night in this state.

ANO-2013.explanation_text: The hour before the spike shows almost no consumption at all, followed immediately by a single hour containing roughly the missing energy plus the normal amount, then a clean return to typical levels. That is the signature of a meter that briefly stopped recording and then reported the accumulated total in the next reading. No action is needed on the refrigeration equipment itself, though the metering link is worth a check.

ANO-2014.explanation_text:
The reading jumped to many times what this refrigeration zone can physically draw for exactly one hour, then returned to normal immediately with no lead-up or recovery period. Real refrigeration problems build up and stay elevated while the system struggles, which is not what happened here. This is almost certainly a bad meter reading rather than an equipment issue, so no technician visit is needed 
beyond flagging the meter for a data check.

ANO-2015.explanation_text: The unit jumped sharply to several times its normal draw and then stayed well above normal for hours rather than settling back down. Outdoor conditions were mild, so cooling demand cannot explain the extra load, and the step-change pattern points to the air-moving side of the unit struggling or failed, forcing the system to run hard continuously. This warrants a technician visit before the unit is damaged further or fails outright.

ANO-2016.explanation_text: The unit's power draw jumped almost immediately to roughly three and a half times its normal level and then stayed flat there for eight hours without settling back down. Cold outdoor conditions cannot explain this, and the sudden step-and-hold shape is typical of a fan or drive running continuously against a problem rather than cycling normally. This should be treated as a genuine equipment fault and a technician sent to inspect the unit.

ANO-2017.explanation_text: Energy use on this refrigeration zone jumped sharply on a cool Sunday evening, when there is no production activity and no weather demand to explain it, then kept climbing steadily for several hours instead of settling back down. That escalating pattern is typical of a cooling system losing capacity and running harder and harder to hold temperature, most often from a slow loss of refrigerant. A technician should be sent, as continued running in this state risks product temperature excursions and further damage to the equipment.

ANO-2018.explanation_text: The extra load builds through the afternoon, moves up and down rather than holding steady, and falls back to normal levels once the busy period ends. That rise-and-recovery shape is what we see when the zone is worked hard during peak activity, with frequent door openings and restocking making the cooling equipment run more often. Outdoor conditions were mild, so weather is not driving it, and nothing suggests failing equipment; no dispatch is needed, but if the same afternoon pattern persists all week it is worth a quick check of door discipline and cooling performance.

ANO-2019.explanation_text: Refrigeration load climbed sharply in the early morning and then held at a high, flat level for about three hours before falling back — a pattern typical of cooling equipment struggling and running far harder than needed to hold temperature. The outdoor air was cold at the time, so weather cannot explain the extra energy, and there is no matching increase in site activity. This points to a problem with the cooling unit itself in Zone B and warrants a technician visit before it worsens or puts stored product at risk.

ANO-2020.explanation_text: The refrigeration load rose modestly through the late afternoon, held for about two hours, and then fell back below its normal level on its own. Equipment problems in refrigeration typically stay elevated until repaired rather than settling down by themselves, and the cold outdoor conditions rule out any weather-driven cooling demand. The pattern matches the busiest stretch of the working day, with more product movement and door activity making the units work harder before end-of-day quiet. No dispatch needed, but worth a quick check that the zone held temperature during the busy window.
